title: Granny stripe baby blanket
subtitle: A simple stripe worked row by row in treble clusters.
excerpt: Rows of treble clusters in alternating colours make a fast, stretchy baby blanket in DK cotton. No joining, no motifs, just one long stripe after another.
sourceNotes: Stripe construction draws on the Victorian striped afghan tradition documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (2nd series, 1880s, Internet Archive). Treble-cluster stripe is a modern simplification of the Victorian long-stitch strip.

glossaryTerms.definition: The chains worked at the start of a row to bring the hook up to the height of the new row's stitches. For trebles, the turning chain is three chains.
Swapping to a new yarn colour by pulling the new colour through the final loop of the last stitch in the old colour.
Threading yarn tails through nearby stitches with the tapestry needle so the fabric holds without knots showing.

crochet.gaugeText: 16 tr × 8 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked.

content.text: A granny stripe baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. Each row is a strip of treble clusters. The colours swap every row to build up the stripe.
The clusters are three trebles into the same chain space, the same move as a granny square corner. Each

happens at the end of a row, keeping the join on the wrong side. The finished fabric is stretchy and machine-washable. At the stated gauge it drapes a standard cot mattress lengthways with a little overhang.

items.name: DK cotton yarn, Colour A
items.substitutions: Any smooth DK cotton or cotton-acrylic blend.

content.text: 16 tr x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked. Work a 20-stitch swatch across 10 rows to check. If your swatch comes out wider than 10 cm, go down a hook size; if narrower, go up. At this gauge the blanket reaches 75 x 90 cm. A gauge drift of one stitch per 10 cm adds or removes about 6 cm on the width.
tr (UK) / dc (US): treble, one yarn-over before inserting hook, three loops worked off two at a time
gr-cl: granny cluster, three trebles into the same chain space
Foundation chain: using Colour A, chain 121. This makes 40 clusters across plus a turning chain at each end.

of 3 ch (counts as first tr). Skip the first 3 ch. *Work 3 tr into the next ch space (one gr-cl made), ch 1, skip 1 ch*. Repeat from * to * to last 3 ch. Work 3 tr into last ch space. Turn. (40 gr-cl, 39 ch-1 spaces.)

Join Colour B to the ch-3 turning chain of Row 1. Ch 3. *Work 3 tr into the next ch-1 space, ch 1*. Repeat across. Work 1 tr into the top of the turning chain. Turn. Cut Colour A leaving a 15 cm tail. (40 gr-cl.)
Join Colour C. Work as Row 2. Cut Colour B. (40 gr-cl.)
Continue working one row per colour in the order A, B, C, A, B, C. Work 72 rows total (24 repeats of the three-colour stripe). Fasten off.

For a wider blanket: add stitches in multiples of 4 to the foundation chain. For a longer blanket: work more rows. Each 3-row stripe adds about 3.5 cm in height at this gauge. A single-bed size (90 x 120 cm) needs a foundation chain of 157 and 102 rows.
Thread all tails with the tapestry needle, running each one along the row edges.
along the stripe edges hides the tails in the fold. Block lightly with a steam iron on the wool setting held 2 cm above the fabric if the edges curl.
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle. Reshape while damp. Dry flat. Do not tumble dry cotton; it shrinks and distorts the stripe alignment.
Work the same stripe in DK acrylic for a warmer throw with easier care. Or try the ripple blanket pattern, which adds a gentle zigzag to the same treble-cluster base.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: What goes wrong on a first stripe blanket.

items.fix: Work the turning chain on a hook size larger, or add an extra chain at the turn.

items.cause: Skipping the turn chain at row ends
items.fix: Count the turning chain as the first treble and work the final cluster of each row into the top of the previous row's turning chain.

items.symptom: Colour joins visible on right side
items.cause: Joining new colour on right-side row
items.fix: Always join new colours at the end of the wrong-side row so the knot lands on the back.
